strengths: MaskSub provides a simple, technically coherent way to incorporate strong masking into supervised training. Shared parameters and detached prediction targets avoid a separate teacher and additional inference cost. Its demonstrated practical benefits support weak acceptance despite the conceptual and interpretive limitations below.

The central ImageNet results are convincing. Table 1 reports improvements of 0.3–0.7 percentage points across ViT sizes and training schedules using strong DeiT-III recipes. Table A.13 provides three-run statistics supporting the ViT-S/B improvements; for ViT-B, accuracy increases from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02.

The paper meaningfully addresses training cost. Table 8 shows ViT-B achieving 84.1% in 25 GPU days versus 83.7% in 26 GPU days for longer baseline training. Table 9 also reports better accuracy than CoSub with substantially lower measured cost. These comparisons establish value beyond simply adding computation.

Validation is unusually broad: pretrained-model finetuning, ResNet and Swin, transfer classification, segmentation, detection, robustness, and language-related experiments. For example, ADE20K single-scale mIoU improves from 48.8 to 49.4 for ViT-B, while ImageNet-A accuracy improves from 36.8 to 41.9. This supports usefulness beyond ImageNet validation accuracy.

The appendix strengthens the evidence with distillation-loss ablations, masking-ratio and loss-weight sweeps, and repeated runs. Table A.6 supports the importance of the distillation component. The concise algorithm, detailed vision training configurations, and provided code link also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited, and the distinction from consistency learning is overstated. With a detached teacher distribution q, CE(q,p) equals KL(q||p) plus an entropy term that contributes no gradient. Consequently, Section 2's distinction between MaskSub's distillation loss and UDA-style consistency loss does not establish a new objective. The stronger contribution is the effective use of masking and token removal within supervised training recipes.

The proposed 'automatic difficulty control' mechanism is only partially established. The loss and gradient-norm curves support improved optimization, but do not isolate this explanation from ordinary consistency regularization. Equation (3) also does not apply masking exclusively to correctly predicted examples, as the discussion suggests: confidently incorrect predictions remain distillation targets.

Benefits are task dependent. In Table A.10, adding MaskSub during finetuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89 to 89.55. Section 4.2 explicitly reports unchanged best-checkpoint accuracy for CLIP finetuning, despite improved final-epoch accuracy. Moreover, hierarchical architectures require roughly twice the training computation. These findings qualify the broad claims of consistently beneficial, efficient application.

Some comparative claims have weaker support than the main DeiT-III results. Table 6 mixes architectures and training recipes for several self-distillation baselines, although selected methods are re-evaluated under RSB; it therefore does not establish broad incompatibility of competing methods with modern recipes. Likewise, small gains such as BEiTv2's 0.1 points and COCO's 0.2–0.3 AP lack reported variability, so their individual reliability remains uncertain.

Minor presentation issues should be distinguished from the scientific reservations: Table 7 labels both CIFAR columns as CIFAR100, and the claim of a fixed 50% masking ratio across all experiments conflicts with the explicitly stated 15% BERT setting. These are readily correctable and do not determine the recommendation.
